authoringProvenance.author: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Pro — candidate authoring assistant

items.prompt: A proposed O(n) sliding-window solution fails a supplied counterexample with negative values. A proven O(n log n) alternative satisfies the output contract and the maximum constraints. What is the correct strategy decision?
constraints: The O(n) candidate fails a valid counterexample.
The O(n log n) candidate is proven correct.
O(n log n) fits the maximum constraints.

options.text: Use the proven O(n log n) strategy; the faster candidate is not eligible until its correctness gap is resolved.
Use the O(n) strategy because its lower growth rate should dominate, and treat the supplied failing case as an exceptional input.
Run both candidates, then combine their outputs by choosing the shorter reported range whenever they disagree on the answer.

feedback.reason: Correctness is a feasibility gate. A strategy that violates the output contract is not a faster solution to the same problem.

blocks.text: Optimization compares implementations only after they compute the required function. The counterexample establishes that the window candidate's invariant is insufficient under the stated value domain, so its O(n) running time describes a different, incorrect procedure. The proven O(n log n) candidate fits the constraints and therefore remains eligible. The faster idea may be revisited by changing its state or proof, but it cannot be selected on asymptotics alone. The transfer rule is to treat correctness, legality, and resource feasibility as gates before ranking speed.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.choose_asymptotic: A wrong result is not an acceptable constant-probability or edge-case trade-off unless the product explicitly permits approximation. This option becomes valid only after the candidate is proven correct for the complete domain.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.average_outputs: Combining incompatible outputs has no correctness argument and can hide both defects. Cross-checking is useful for testing, but production selection still needs a defined correct result.

items.prompt: A pair-sum task must return two distinct original indices whose values sum to T. An in-place sort followed by two pointers is fast but loses the required identity mapping; sorting indexed records is slightly slower and uses more memory but fits all limits. Which candidate should be selected?
constraints: Return original indices.
Duplicate values may exist.
The indexed strategy fits time and space limits.

options.text: Sort in place and reconstruct indices by searching for equal values afterward without retained identity.
Select the in-place sort because returning the right values is close enough to returning their indices.
Select the indexed-record strategy because it preserves the required witnesses.

feedback.reason: The witness contract is part of correctness. The legal adaptation that preserves original identity must be evaluated, even when it costs more.

blocks.text: A strategy is not correct merely because it finds two values with the right sum. The caller asks for positions in the original input, and duplicates can make value-only reconstruction ambiguous. Sorting indexed pairs retains that information explicitly, at the cost of O(n) auxiliary records and the same O(n log n) dominant sort. When those resources fit, preserving the output contract takes priority over an illegal in-place shortcut. The transfer rule is to preserve every required witness, ordering, multiplicity, and provenance field before optimizing representation.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.raw_sort_fast: Returning values instead of original indices changes the function being computed. It becomes valid only if the output contract is relaxed to values or input mutation and identity loss are explicitly allowed.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.guess_indices: Duplicate values make post-hoc identity ambiguous, and an additional search can choose the same position twice. Reconstruction is valid only with a retained one-to-one mapping and a proof that handles multiplicity.

items.prompt: Order the steps for optimizing a correct reference solution without allowing performance work to redefine the problem.
constraints: A correct reference can be executed on bounded cases.
The optimized mechanism must preserve the same output contract.
Ordering is scored by adjacent relations.

elements.text: Fix the output contract and executable reference behaviour on small cases.
State the candidate invariant and prove equivalence to the required result.
Confirm the reference misses a real resource constraint or measured bottleneck.
Replace repeated work while preserving the proof obligations and regression oracle.

feedback.reason: Correct semantics anchor the process, performance evidence identifies what must change, and proof obligations precede replacement. Optimization then targets demonstrated cost without discarding the reference oracle.

blocks.text: A safe optimization process follows the evidence dependencies:

items: Fix the observable output contract and keep a simple correct reference that can generate expected results on bounded inputs.
Measure the reference or apply the maximum constraints to identify a real time, space, or latency failure and the exact work that causes it.
Design the candidate invariant, compressed state, discard rule, or preprocessing and prove that it preserves the reference result for the complete domain.
Implement the replacement, remove the demonstrated repeated work, and continue differential regression checks against the reference on edge and randomized bounded cases.

blocks.text: Measurement precedes candidate proof because it identifies what actually needs to change; proof precedes replacement because speed cannot establish equivalence. The sequence prevents a fast heuristic from silently becoming the new specification. Any optimization that changes observable semantics or lacks an equivalence argument returns to the proof step.

items.prompt: For n ≤ 50,000, a proven O(n log n) sorting-based solution fits comfortably. A proposed O(n) greedy rule has no invariant or exchange argument and has not been tested beyond examples. Which choice is responsible?
constraints: n is at most 50,000.
O(n log n) fits the limit.
The O(n) rule has no proof and only example coverage.

options.text: Use the proven O(n log n) solution; investigate the linear rule separately until it has a correctness argument.
Use the O(n) rule because its lower asymptotic bound should take priority even before the irreversible greedy choices are justified.
Use the O(n) rule because matching every provided example is sufficient evidence that its local choices generalize to the full input domain.

feedback.reason: When a proven strategy satisfies the constraints, an unproven optimization is unnecessary risk. Lower asymptotic time does not establish semantic equivalence.

blocks.text: The decision is not between elegance and caution; it is between one complete contract and one incomplete hypothesis. O(n log n) at the stated scale is feasible, while the greedy candidate lacks the property that would justify its irreversible choices. Examples exercise only a tiny subset of inputs and often miss adversarial orderings or ties. The linear idea can become preferable after a proof and boundary analysis, but until then it is not a production candidate. The transfer rule is to stop optimizing once a simple proven method satisfies the real constraints, unless a measured requirement demands more.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.linear_label: Complexity describes resource growth for the implemented rule; it does not prove the rule returns the right answer. This becomes valid only after correctness is independently established.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.examples_prove: Examples confirm a few instances, not universal behaviour. They become meaningful evidence only as part of broader tests and a proof that covers the full domain.

items.prompt: Prefix sums may reach 10^14. Two implementations are both O(n + q): one stores 32-bit signed totals and can overflow; the other stores 64-bit totals and fits the stated range. Which implementation is eligible?
constraints: Reachable totals may be 10^14.
The required result is ordinary integer arithmetic, not modular arithmetic.
Both implementations have the same asymptotic cost.

options.text: Use 64-bit totals because the numeric domain is part of correctness.
Use 32-bit totals and rely on wraparound to preserve range differences.
Use 32-bit totals because the smaller type may be faster.

feedback.reason: Asymptotic equality does not make overflowing arithmetic correct. The representation must cover all reachable intermediate and final values.

blocks.text: A prefix sum can exceed every individual input value because it accumulates many terms. A signed 32-bit integer ranges from −2^31 to 2^31 − 1, approximately ±2.1·10^9, so it cannot represent 10^14. A signed 64-bit integer reaches about ±9.22·10^18 and covers the stated bound. If a runtime wraps 32-bit overflow, it preserves arithmetic modulo 2^32 rather than ordinary integer sums; other language models may trap or leave signed overflow undefined. In every case the narrow implementation violates this contract. The 64-bit version has the same asymptotic cost and correct range. The transfer rule is to prove bounds for intermediate state before micro-optimizing type width or arithmetic.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.narrow_faster: A possible constant-factor benefit cannot justify incorrect values. This becomes valid only if a proven tighter bound keeps every intermediate within 32-bit range.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.overflow_wrap: Modular wraparound computes a different algebra. It is legal only when the problem specifies the same modulus and subtraction is interpreted consistently under it.

items.prompt: An optimized implementation matches the sample cases but changes several state updates from a correct reference. Which evidence is strongest before replacing the reference?
constraints: A correct reference implementation exists.
The optimized version changes internal state updates.
Sample cases are not exhaustive.

options.text: Use agreement on the published sample cases as the equivalence test, because those examples represent the important boundary conditions.
Use a benchmark showing lower time and memory as the replacement evidence, because performance improvement is the goal of the rewrite.
A preserved invariant plus differential tests against the reference across edge and randomized bounded cases.

feedback.reason: Replacement needs evidence of semantic equivalence, not only speed or sample agreement. Proof obligations and an independent oracle catch different classes of defects.

blocks.text: The reference supplies executable expected behaviour for inputs small enough to handle, while the invariant explains why the optimized state summarizes the same necessary information. Differential testing can expose boundary, duplicate, and update-order errors that examples omit; the proof guards against merely failing to sample a counterexample. A benchmark measures cost only after correctness is established. The transfer rule is to preserve an independent oracle whenever optimization compresses state, skips work, reorders operations, or introduces amortization.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.samples_only: Samples are sparse illustrations and commonly omit adversarial boundaries. They become sufficient only for a truly finite contract that explicitly enumerates every possible input.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.benchmark_only: A faster wrong implementation is not an optimization of the same function. Benchmarking becomes decision evidence after equivalence has been established.

items.prompt: An optimization returns the correct numeric score but omits the required original indices and changes the tie policy. How should it be classified?

options.text: It is not a valid replacement; matching one output field does not satisfy the complete output contract.
It is equivalent because the primary score is correct and indices are implementation details.
It should replace the reference because output formatting can be repaired later without affecting correctness.
Tie behavior never matters when the score is optimal.

feedback.reason: Correctness is defined by the whole observable contract, including identity and tie behavior, not only one objective value.

blocks.text: Returning a score without the required witnesses cannot satisfy a function that promises indices. Likewise, changing tie policy changes observable behavior when ties are part of the contract. A fast core may be reusable only after it preserves or explicitly adapts every required output and side effect.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.valid_score_equivalence: The omitted indices and altered ties are observable contract violations, not hidden implementation details.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.faster_wins: A later repair is not evidence that the current implementation already returns the promised result.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.tie_irrelevant: Tie semantics are relevant whenever callers or tests observe which equally optimal result is selected.

items.prompt: A linear-time candidate fails one valid edge case, while a quadratic reference passes the full test suite and fits the current maximum n. What is the responsible next step?

options.text: Fix the invariant or reject the linear candidate; retain the correct reference until an optimized replacement is proven.
Exclude the failing edge case because it is uncommon in production data.
Keep the failing candidate because linear asymptotics matter more than one counterexample.
Choose whichever benchmark is faster without investigating the wrong result.

feedback.reason: One valid counterexample disproves correctness, and the stated constraint does not yet require abandoning the correct reference.

blocks.text: The failing input is evidence against the candidate's invariant or boundary handling. First preserve a known-correct implementation, isolate the cause, and prove a repair against edge cases. Only if the repaired or alternate strategy meets the actual maximum constraints should performance change the selection.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.hide_edge_case: Valid inputs cannot be removed from the contract to protect an implementation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.keep_broken_for_scale: Asymptotic speed does not compensate for returning a wrong answer on an allowed input.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.benchmark_both_only: Performance comparison is meaningful only among semantically equivalent implementations.

items.prompt: An algorithm is mathematically correct but needs O(n) extra memory, while the problem limit permits only O(1) auxiliary space. Which decision follows?

options.text: It is ineligible under the stated contract; correctness includes resource bounds, so another valid strategy or a contract change is required.
It is accepted because resource limits are performance suggestions rather than correctness conditions.
Count the auxiliary array as input storage because it contains copied input values.
Call the memory O(1) because the element type has fixed size.

feedback.reason: A solution must meet hard time, space, mutation, and output constraints together; mathematical result correctness alone is insufficient.

blocks.text: If the contract limits auxiliary space to constant, an input-sized index is a disqualifying resource violation even if every returned value is correct. The analysis must state what memory is counted and whether the platform permits in-place mutation, streaming, or a different representation. Renaming or reclassifying a copied array does not change its asymptotic size.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.correct_means_accepted: Hard resource constraints are part of the problem contract and can make a mathematically correct method unusable.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.hide_memory: Copied input-sized storage is auxiliary memory unless the contract explicitly grants it as workspace.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.claim_constant: Fixed element size does not make the number of stored elements constant.

items.prompt: Select all gates that should pass before replacing a correct baseline with a faster implementation.

options.text: The optimized implementation preserves outputs, edge cases, tie rules, and permitted side effects.
Its invariant is explained and it agrees with an independent reference on targeted and randomized cases.
Its time, space, numeric representation, and input-size behavior fit the stated limits.
It is faster on a few samples, even if the output contract and proof have not been checked.

feedback.reason: Replacement requires semantic equivalence, a correctness argument or oracle evidence, and resource feasibility; benchmark wins are downstream of those gates.

blocks.text: The baseline is an executable oracle for bounded differential tests, while the optimized invariant explains why compressed state or skipped work remains safe. The replacement must also meet numeric, memory, mutation, and maximum-input constraints. Samples can support performance investigation but cannot waive failed correctness gates.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.faster_sample: Sample speed is not evidence of correct behavior or feasibility at the maximum constraints.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.same_observable_contract: A faster function with different observable semantics is not a replacement.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.invariant_or_oracle: Correctness must be supported by proof and/or independent comparison, especially when state updates change.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.fits_constraints: A solution that exceeds a hard limit is not eligible even if it is mathematically correct.

items.prompt: What should be established before optimizing a candidate algorithm's inner loop?
constraints: The candidate has a claimed output contract.
The optimization may change state transitions.

options.text: State the invariant and prove that the optimized transition preserves it and the required output.
options.explanation: Optimization is safe only relative to a correctness argument.

options.text: Benchmark the code before defining what it must compute.
options.explanation: A fast implementation can optimize the wrong result.

options.text: Replace branches with arithmetic regardless of the state invariant.
options.explanation: Removing branches can change boundary behavior.

options.text: Defer empty and boundary cases until after performance work is complete.
options.explanation: Optimizations often expose exactly those cases.

feedback.reason: A local speedup is meaningful only if it preserves the algorithm's semantic invariant.

blocks.text: The invariant describes what the state means at every step. Any loop fusion, shortcut, or data-structure change must be checked against it before performance numbers are trusted.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.benchmark_first: A fast implementation can optimize the wrong result.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.micro_optimize: Removing branches can change boundary behavior.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.ignore_edges: Optimizations often expose exactly those cases.

items.prompt: A proposed optimization is faster but fails one legal input. What is the correct status?
constraints: The input satisfies the public constraints.
The output differs from the required answer.

options.text: Reject or repair the optimization; one legal counterexample is sufficient to invalidate universal correctness.
options.explanation: Performance cannot compensate for an incorrect result.

options.text: Keep it because the speedup is larger than the cost of one failing case.
options.explanation: A universal contract has no allowance for arbitrary legal failures.

options.text: Label the input rare and leave the implementation unchanged.
options.explanation: Metadata does not fix a correctness defect.

options.text: The algorithm is correct until more failures are found.
options.explanation: The first valid failure already disproves the claim.

feedback.reason: Correctness is a gate, not a weighted score against runtime.

blocks.text: A legal counterexample means the optimized algorithm does not implement the stated function. Restore the invariant or choose a different optimization before comparing performance.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.keep_if_fast: A universal contract has no allowance for arbitrary legal failures.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.mark_rare: Metadata does not fix a correctness defect.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.increase_tests: The first valid failure already disproves the claim.

items.prompt: Why must numeric range analysis precede an asymptotic optimization that changes arithmetic order?
constraints: The implementation uses finite-width integers.
Intermediate values may be larger than the final answer.

options.text: The reordered expression must preserve exact arithmetic without overflow; otherwise an asymptotically faster path can return incorrect values.
options.explanation: Machine arithmetic is part of correctness.

options.text: Check only whether the final mathematical answer fits; intermediate overflow cannot affect it.
options.explanation: Overflow can occur before later cancellation or reduction.

options.text: Asymptotic notation guarantees that integer operations are exact.
options.explanation: Big-O says nothing about numeric range.

options.text: Cast the final result to a wider type after narrow operations.
options.explanation: Lost bits cannot be recovered after overflow.

feedback.reason: Arithmetic order is a semantic decision under finite machine types.

blocks.text: A transformation valid over unbounded integers may be invalid in the implementation domain. Widen before risky operations or prove bounded intermediates as part of the optimization review.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.final_only: Overflow can occur before later cancellation or reduction.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.big_o_proof: Big-O says nothing about numeric range.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.cast_after: Lost bits cannot be recovered after overflow.

items.prompt: What is the safest first question when optimizing a routine that currently handles nonempty inputs?
constraints: The public contract may allow empty inputs.
The optimized loop assumes an initial element.

options.text: Define and test the empty-input output before applying the optimization, so initialization and identity values remain correct.
options.explanation: Empty cases expose missing state initialization.

options.text: Assume the caller never supplies empty input because the existing loop starts at index zero.
options.explanation: An unstated assumption is not a contract.

options.text: Insert a synthetic zero element to make the loop uniform.
options.explanation: Padding can change the mathematical result.

options.text: Optimize the common nonempty path and let the empty case fall through.
options.explanation: A fall-through can become an exception or a wrong result.

feedback.reason: Boundary semantics must be explicit before loop initialization is changed.

blocks.text: An identity value, empty collection, error, or unavailable state may be correct depending on the API. The optimization must preserve that decision rather than silently manufacturing an input.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.reject_empty: An unstated assumption is not a contract.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.pad_empty: Padding can change the mathematical result.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.optimize_nonempty_only: A fall-through can become an exception or a wrong result.
